sections.body:
A car breakdown is an unplanned stop in which your car can no longer be driven safely. The engine has stopped, or the car will not move, and the cause may be something you could fix in ten minutes or something that needs a recovery vehicle. Knowing which one you have matters, because the first ten minutes decide whether the breakdown is a small nuisance or an expensive day.

Most breakdowns on the road are boring. The commonest causes are a flat tyre, an empty fuel tank, a flat battery, an engine that has overheated and switched itself off, a door that will not latch, and a broken belt or hose. Failures in the engine and the gearbox are rarer, and they are also the ones most likely to need a tow.

A breakdown is not an accident. An accident is damage caused by a collision, and it involves other people, insurance and possibly the police. A breakdown happens to one vehicle on its own. The confusion between the two causes real trouble, because a breakdown handled as an accident can mean hours of waiting for the wrong kind of help.

The first five minutes matter. In those minutes you stop safely, protect the scene, and find out three things: where exactly you are, what the car is telling you, and what help is available to you. Everything else in this article follows from those three answers.

Do one thing at a time, and do it in the right order. If you try to fix the car before the road is safe, a small fault becomes a serious one. If you call for help before you know where you are, the operator will ask you anyway, and the delay costs time.

Most of what you need on a roadside is small and cheap: a warning triangle, a reflective jacket, a torch, a power bank, water and a spare set of keys. A breakdown is far more unpleasant on a dark road in the rain than in a car park at midday, and the difference is almost entirely about preparation.

Whatever the cause, you are entitled to professional help, and in most countries your breakdown assistance membership or your insurance provides some of it. Knowing what your membership covers before you need it saves the awkward part of the conversation later.
examples: The engine has stopped and the car will not move, so I need roadside assistance.
I am not sure whether this is a breakdown or something I can fix, but I cannot continue safely.
sections.heading: What a breakdown is, and what the first five minutes decide

sections.body:
The instinct is to get out and look at the engine. Resist it for a minute, because a stationary car with no warning is the most dangerous thing you can leave on a road. Every step here comes before every step about the fault.

Switch on the hazard warning lights and stop the engine. They tell the traffic behind you that something is wrong, and they stop you causing a second, much worse incident.

Then move the car as far out of the way as you can. On a dual carriageway this means the hard shoulder, and further along it if you can manage. On a street it means a drive, a lay-by or a quiet side road. If the car will roll, push it with the steering on and the handbrake released, and use the hazard lights while you do. If it will not move, do not force it; switch the hazards on and leave it where it is.

Set out your warning triangle. Put it behind the car on the road, on the driver's side, so a driver sees it before the car. The usual distance is about 100 metres on a motorway and 25 metres on an ordinary road, but a triangle placed too far away is better than one placed too close.

Get everyone out of the car and away from the traffic. Stand behind a barrier or a wall if there is one. Never stand on a motorway or in a live lane, and never stand in front of the car. A car rolling downhill will travel further than you expect.

If you are on a motorway, leave the carriageway completely and make the call from a safe place, or use the emergency telephone if you cannot safely get back to a phone. Follow the signs to the emergency phone, and note the location marker they show you.

Finally, keep everyone together and keep phones charged. Two people with working phones are worth more than one person with a full battery.
examples: I have moved the car onto the hard shoulder and switched the hazards on.
We are standing behind the barrier until the recovery vehicle arrives.
sections.heading: Make the road safe before you touch the car
steps: Switch on the hazard warning lights and stop the engine.
Move the car as far off the carriageway as you can.
Place the warning triangle behind the car on the road.
Get everyone out and stand well away, behind a barrier if there is one.
Make the call from a safe place, not from the carriageway.

sections.body:
Roadside operators work from a script and a map. Give them four things, in this order, and the call goes quickly.

First, **where you are**. Road name, direction of travel, and the nearest junction with its number. Add the distance to it, and a landmark that will not move: a petrol station, a big sign, a bridge, a petrol price board. On a motorway, give the number and the direction, and say which side of the road you are on. An operator who cannot find you will send the nearest patrol, and the nearest patrol may be a long drive away from you.

Second, **what the car is doing**. Say whether the engine is off, whether the steering and brakes still work, and whether the car can be pushed. These facts decide whether a recovery vehicle can lift your car or must tow it with a wheel on the ground.

Third, **what the car is telling you**. Name the warning light rather than describing the colour of the light vaguely. "The engine warning light is on" is useful. "A red light is flashing" is not. Give the fuel level, the battery condition, and whether the car restarts if you turn the key.

Fourth, **what you have already tried and what you need**. If you have changed the wheel and the replacement is flat too, say so. If you need a jump start, a fuel drop, a wheel change or a tow, say which one. Then ask the questions you need answered: the estimated arrival time, the price, whether your policy or membership covers it, whether to wait in the car or in a café, and whether they will ask you to sign anything.

Speak clearly, but do not shout at the phone. If the line is bad, repeat your location first, because that is the part they cannot guess. If the operator asks you to hold, stay on the line if you can, and keep your phone charged.

And if you speak a second language, say so at the start. Many operators can continue in another language, and those who cannot will usually get you someone who can.
examples: Hello, I am on the A12 heading east, about two kilometres before junction 14, opposite a petrol station.
My dashboard shows the engine warning light, and the steering and brakes still work.
Could you tell me the likely arrival time and whether this is covered by my insurance?
The fuel gauge is still above a quarter, so I do not think it is out of fuel.
sections.heading: Describing the problem so the right help is sent

sections.body:
These are the words you will hear on the phone and you will need to understand when they are said to you.

A **breakdown** is the stop itself, not the fault. People use the word for both, so "I have had a breakdown" might mean the car stopped or that the gearbox failed. A **fault** is the specific fault, and it is what tells the operator what to send.

Roadside assistance is the service that comes to you. It may be included in your insurance, sold by the manufacturer with the car, or bought as a separate membership. A **patrol** or a **recovery vehicle** is the van or truck that arrives.

A **call-out** is one visit. Some policies include a call-out fee and a fixed amount of work, and then charge per kilometre beyond that. **Towing** or **recovery** means the car is carried to a garage, and **towing** in the strict sense means a rope or a lift.

The **hazard warning lights** are the two orange indicators you switch on together. The **warning triangle** is the red reflective triangle you place on the road. A **high-visibility jacket** is the fluorescent vest that makes you visible at night.

A **jump start** is starting the car with the battery of another car. A **flat battery** is a battery that has lost its charge, usually because it is old, because the lights were left on, or because the car stood for weeks.
sections.heading: The words of a breakdown call

terms.example: I have had a breakdown on the motorway, and I need a recovery vehicle.
terms.gloss: An unplanned stop in which the car cannot be driven safely. It is the stop, not the specific fault that caused it.

terms.example: Do you know whether my roadside assistance covers a call-out in this area?
terms.gloss: The service that comes to help a broken-down car. It comes through insurance, a manufacturer package or a separate membership.

terms.example: The recovery vehicle will lift the car, so I do not need to empty the boot.
terms.gloss: The van or truck sent to collect the car. Some can lift a car and some can only tow it on a wheel.

terms.example: Switch the hazard lights on before you get out of the car.
terms.gloss: The pair of orange indicators switched on together to warn traffic that a vehicle is stopped or slow.

terms.example: Put the warning triangle out about 100 metres behind the car.
terms.gloss: The red reflective triangle placed on the road behind a stopped vehicle so drivers see it in time.

terms.example: Could you send someone to jump start the car? The battery is flat.
terms.gloss: Starting a car with a flat battery by connecting it to the battery of another car with cables.

sections.body:
First, standing in a live traffic lane to look at the engine. Move to safety first, always.

Second, leaving the hazard lights off while you make a phone call. The lights cost nothing and they are the only thing that tells the traffic behind you what is happening.

Third, opening the bonnet on an overheated engine without waiting. The coolant may be above 100 °C and will scald you badly when it meets the air. Wait at least twenty minutes.

Fourth, accepting a tow from someone you did not call. Check that the vehicle is marked with a company name and a telephone number before you get in it, and tell someone where you are going.

Fifth, leaving children or passengers in a car on a live road, or letting them stand in the traffic with you. They belong with the adults, behind the barrier, every time.
sections.heading: Five things that turn a breakdown into a real danger

sections.body:
Most drivers are grateful for help, and most helpers are unwilling to offer it, because they are not sure what to do. The steps below are the ordinary, safe way to help. Read them once now, so that the next time you can act without thinking.

The first rule is that your own safety comes first, and it comes before politeness. You cannot help anyone from inside a hospital, and you cannot help anyone if you are the second casualty. If the road is fast, if it is dark, if it is raining hard, or if you are not trained, then a phone call is the better help.

When you do stop, approach the scene in a way that the driver can see you coming. Keep your hazards on so your car is visible, and put on a high-visibility jacket if you have one in the boot.

Look for danger before you look for a fault. Traffic, fire, fuel, electricity and unstable vehicles are all more urgent than a flat tyre. If the driver is hurt, or if there is any fire, or if the accident involves a lorry, call the emergency services first and give them the location in the same format you would give the roadside operator.

Then offer what you can. Most people need one of three things: a phone call to their assistance line, a warning triangle or reflective jacket, or a warning triangle and a light. If you have a jump-start kit, use it only if you know how. If you are not sure how, an honest "I can call someone for you" is worth more than a wrong attempt.

Stay until the professional help arrives if the driver is alone and worried. A person sitting in a broken car on a dark road is a frightened person, and company is a real service.
examples: I have stopped to help. I am on the hard shoulder with my hazards on.
Are you hurt? Shall I call an ambulance for you?
sections.heading: If you stop to help another driver
steps: Only stop if you can do it without putting yourself in danger.
Switch on your hazards, pull in as far as possible and put on a high-visibility jacket.
Look for danger to life before you look at the fault.
Call the emergency services first if anyone is hurt or there is a fire.
Offer the help you actually understand, such as making the call or passing over a warning triangle.
Stay with the driver until professional help arrives.

sections.body:
Some faults are yours to fix at the roadside, and some are not. Here is how to tell them apart.

A **flat tyre** is the most common roadside job. If the car is on a hard shoulder or in a safe place, and you have the correct wheel and a working jack, you can change it in about half an hour. If the spare is a temporary repair kit, the speed limit on it is printed on the kit, usually 80 km/h, and you should not drive far on it. Tighten the wheel nuts in a star pattern, not one after another, and recheck them after the first fifty kilometres. If you cannot find a safe place to work, do not attempt it. Call for help.

A **flat battery** can often be solved by a jump start, and the cost of a call-out is far higher than the cost of a set of cables. Connect the positive terminal first, then the negative, and remove them in the reverse order. Never let the cables touch. Do not jump start a battery that is swollen, leaking or frozen, because it may go into the car, and give the engine a moment to charge before you try to drive off.

An **overheated engine** is a warning, not a fault to be ignored. Pull over at once, switch the engine off, and leave it for at least twenty minutes. Never open the radiator cap or the expansion tank while it is hot. If the temperature warning light stays on once the engine has cooled, or if the coolant level is low, you do not drive on. You tow.

An **empty fuel tank** is simple if you can find fuel and carry it safely. Put enough in to reach a petrol station and no more. Do not carry a container of petrol in the passenger compartment, and do not smoke or use a flame anywhere near it.

Some faults are not yours at all: a smell of fuel, a burning smell, smoke, a warning light that says **stop**, a knocking noise, or a smell of hot metal. In those cases, get out, get away from the car and call for the fire service as well as for help.
examples: The engine has overheated and I am going to leave it to cool for twenty minutes.
I have a spare wheel and a jack, so I can change the tyre if the car is safe to work on.
The battery is flat, but I have a jump-start kit in the boot.
sections.heading: When the car can be pushed, towed or driven

sections.body:
Call the emergency number in your country first: 113 for police and traffic, 115 for ambulance in Vietnam, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the United Kingdom and 911 in the United States. Say where you are in the same format you would use for roadside assistance, and say what has happened.

For heavy bleeding, press hard on the wound with a clean cloth or your hand and keep pressing. Do not lift the cloth to look.

Do not move an injured person unless they are in danger where they are, such as in a live lane or in a burning car. A person with a neck or back injury can be made much worse by being moved.

Keep the person warm and calm. Sit them down, cover them, and talk to them. Fear is often worse than the injury.

If someone is trapped, do not pull them out unless you have to. A badly damaged car can move under pressure. Wait for the fire and rescue service.
sections.heading: If a person is hurt

sections.body:
The ten minutes after the help arrives are worth as much as the ten minutes before it, because that is when the evidence is still fresh.

Photograph everything. The scene, the damage, the position of your car on the road, the other vehicles, the signs and landmarks, the fuel gauge, the odometer and the warning lights. Take them before anything is moved. If the recovery vehicle has already arrived, photograph where the car was sitting and how it was marked.

Write down the timeline while you still remember it. The time of the failure, the time you called, the time the operator gave you as the arrival time, the time the vehicle arrived, the registration of every vehicle involved, and the names of everyone you spoke to. Memory of a stressful hour is unreliable, and a short list written on the back of a receipt will be more useful than an hour of thinking.

Exchange details if other vehicles or people are involved. Name, insurance company, policy number, registration and a telephone number. Do not admit fault, and do not sign anything you have not read. If the other driver is at fault, you will need their details to claim, and if the driver is foreign, the local police may need to be involved.

Keep the receipts and the reference numbers. Photograph the paperwork before you hand it over. Note your case number, and use it every time you speak to the company, because each new call that starts from scratch is a chance for the story to change.

Ask about the storage of the car. If it is going to a garage, ask where the garage is, when they expect to have it, and how you will be told. A car left somewhere unknown is a car you stop paying for.

Tell your insurance company, even when the breakdown is covered by a separate membership. Your insurer may need to open a claim for the car itself, and the two claims often run alongside each other.
examples: My case number is 4471, and the recovery vehicle arrived at 14:20.
I have photographed the scene, the warning lights and the fuel gauge.
Where is the garage, and when will you contact me about the repair?
sections.heading: Afterwards: the insurance call and the notes you keep

item.summary: A breakdown is a conversation you will have while standing on a hard shoulder, so the words matter. After reading this you can make the scene safe, describe the fault in a way that gets the right help sent, say what you need, and look after the people around you until someone arrives.
item.title: What to Say When Your Car Breaks Down
